audit.sub: Where the account is leaking and where the upside is. All figures Klaviyo-attributed unless noted; windows are the last 12 complete months through Jul 2026. This audit covers campaigns and the automation layer, since the two compound together.

wins.title: Build the core flows (welcome, cart, checkout, win-back)
wins.detail: Automated flow revenue is $0. About 160 Add-to-Cart and 140 Checkout-Started events fire monthly (against ~124 orders) with nothing following up, so cart and checkout abandonment are buildable now; a welcome series, post-purchase, and a win-back flow for lapsed customers are the bigger pieces. Browse abandonment needs on-site tracking installed first.

wins.title: Blog-Article campaigns for problem-aware buyers
wins.detail: Campaigns are cannibalising a static list, so the lever is growing it, not just re-segmenting. Educational Blog-Article sends aimed at problem-aware buyers, hosted on-site with a sticky add-to-cart, convert and keep earning organic traffic over time, bringing new people in rather than only spending the existing list.

wins.title: Lift the open rate (22% via welcome + engagement)
wins.detail: Only 22% open. Driving new profiles through a welcome series creates the engagement signal inboxes use to place mail, which lifts opens on the campaigns too. Then send primarily to the engaged.

wins.title: Fix opt-in and rebuild list growth
wins.detail: New subscribers have fallen to single digits a month. Stronger opt-in (popups, lead magnets, post-purchase capture) feeds the welcome flow and every campaign, and the fresh engagement lifts deliverability.

wins.title: Start A/B testing
wins.detail: No experiments have ever run. Testing compounds every other win, so each send beats the last.

wins.title: Connect Recharge & grow Subscribe & Save
wins.detail: Subscribe & Save is live on the store via Recharge but is not wired into Klaviyo (no integration, no subscription events). Connecting it unlocks subscriber segmentation and subscription flows (upcoming charge, failed payment, cancel win-back) and lets email convert one-time buyers to auto-delivery: recurring revenue that does not depend on the next discount.

audit.title: Account audit

findings.body: Every dollar of email revenue here comes from manual campaigns; automated flow revenue over the last 12 months is $0. The buying signals are modest but completely uncaught: about 160 Add-to-Cart and 140 Checkout-Started events a month against roughly 124 orders, so a few dozen abandoned carts and checkouts every month with nothing following up. Cart and checkout abandonment flows can go live now on those Shopify signals; browse-level signals (Viewed Product, Active on Site) barely register, about one event a month, so Klaviyo's on-site tracking is effectively not running and would need setting up before browse abandonment. The bigger pieces are a welcome series for new subscribers, a post-purchase flow, and a win-back flow for lapsed customers (win-back belongs in an automation, not a one-off campaign). Together they turn the automated layer from nothing into a working engine, the highest-ROI revenue in email.

chart.note: Every dollar is manual. The automated half of email, welcome and abandoned cart especially, is not built.

findings.title: There is no automated revenue engine

findings.body: Campaign revenue has almost halved over the year, and the cause is structural: with little or no new traffic coming in (no meaningful top of funnel, and no paid acquisition evident), every send hits the same shrinking, increasingly fatigued list. More sends or tighter segments will not reverse that on their own. Two things will. First, fix the opt-in and welcome experience so new, engaged profiles keep entering. Second, shift some campaigns to Blog-Article sends: educational articles written for problem-aware buyers, hosted on-site so they also earn organic traffic over time, converting through a sticky add-to-cart at the foot of the page. That grows the audience instead of only spending it. The chart shows it plainly: campaign sends hold steady while new subscribers, the list itself, fall from around 40 a month to single digits (about 8 last month). chart.ideasSub: Mostly Blog-Article campaigns, with one valid seasonal sale a month, each a promotion the account has actually run before, alongside them. The articles are problem-aware pieces for the reasons people seek CBD, hosted on-site so they keep earning organic traffic and convert through a sticky add-to-cart. Per-send figures are email-driven estimates; the on-site traffic compounds on top.

findings.title: Campaigns are cannibalising a static list

findings.body: Open rate sits at about 22%, well below a healthy 35 to 45%. Two in three sends are not even opened, which also drags deliverability, so future sends land in spam or the promotions tab. The fix is a loop, not a one-off clean: rebuild the opt-in and welcome experience so new profiles arrive and immediately engage with a welcome series; that fresh engagement is exactly the signal inboxes use to place mail, so it lifts open rates on the campaigns too. Then send primarily to the engaged and re-engage or suppress the rest.

chart.leak: Only 22% open, against a healthy 35 to 45%. Re-engaging the list lifts every send.

findings.title: Only 22% of emails get opened

findings.body: Subscribe & Save runs on the store through Recharge, the recurring-orders portal is live in the site footer, but Recharge is not connected to Klaviyo: there is no Recharge integration and no subscription or recurring-charge events in the account. Three things follow. Email cannot tell a subscriber from a one-time buyer, so nothing is targeted to them. There are no subscription lifecycle flows, no upcoming-charge reminder, failed-payment recovery, or win-back for a cancelled subscription, which is where subscription programs quietly leak. And Subscribe & Save is barely surfaced in email, so few one-time buyers ever convert to it. Because none of the subscription data flows into Klaviyo, its size is not even visible here, which is itself the problem. For an account whose core issue is discounting a static list, recurring revenue is the durable fix: it does not depend on the next sale. Connecting Recharge to Klaviyo, building the subscription flows, and promoting Subscribe & Save is clean, high-leverage work.
findings.title: Subscribe & Save is live but disconnected from Klaviyo

findings.body: We checked the account through Klaviyo's API: there are no A/B experiments in any flow, none running now and none ever set up, so the campaigns cannot get better send over send. The reason our longest-serving accounts keep growing is nonstop testing: six tests a week, three subject-line and preview tests and three full design overhauls, at about a 67% win rate that a central brain, aggregating learnings across every account, keeps pushing higher. Losing tests are cut fast and every winner becomes the new baseline, so each send beats the last instead of being a one-off.
findings.title: No A/B testing — we checked, and nothing is learning

findings.body: Everything in this audit is day-to-day work for us: campaign strategy and cadence, the automated flow architecture, list growth, channel expansion, and relentless testing. The wins at the top are the roadmap. Most of our clients sit between $3M and $20M in revenue, with the average around $5M to $8M, but we also work with smaller budgets. We build a package to fit: a baseline of what we typically do, scaled to where you are.
